overview: Elizabeth I inherited the English throne from her half-sister Mary and restored the Protestant Church of England. During her reign, a rival queen was executed and the English navy beat back a Spanish invasion fleet. Elizabeth never married, and when she died in 1603 the English crown passed to James VI of Scotland.

keyMoments.title: Elizabeth takes the throne
keyMoments.text: Elizabeth was at **Hatfield House** when word came that her half-sister **Mary I** had died. Soon afterward she made **William Cecil** her principal secretary. She asked him to give her the advice he thought best, even when it went against her own wishes.

keyMoments.title: A new settlement for the Church
keyMoments.text: With the **Act of Uniformity**, Parliament restored a revised version of the earlier prayer book. Under Mary I, Parliament had repealed the law that authorized the book. Ministers had to follow the **Book of Common Prayer** in public worship. The Act prescribed imprisonment for a minister convicted of refusing to use the required prayers.

keyMoments.title: Mary, Queen of Scots, is executed
keyMoments.text: Elizabeth signed Mary’s death warrant. The warrant instructed the commissioners to go to **Fotheringhay Castle** and have Mary executed there. Robert Beale, the **Privy Council’s** principal clerk, delivered a copy to the Earl of Kent with a covering letter from the Council ordering the execution. Elizabeth later said she had given no instruction to carry out the warrant.

keyMoments.title: England turns back the Armada
keyMoments.text: English ships fought **Philip II’s Armada**, and bad weather helped scatter the Spanish fleet. In a letter to the queen, **Francis Drake** wrote that the Spanish ships, their sails, ropes and masts needed major repairs. He attributed their condition to the queen’s forces.

deepFacts.text: At Windsor in 1593, Elizabeth translated **Boethius’s The Consolation of Philosophy** into English. Her secretary Thomas Windebank took down prose from her dictation. The surviving draft still has verse in the queen’s own handwriting, including a passage in which Orpheus’s song leaves a hare unafraid of a dog.
